content: Landing pages are specialized web pages designed to organize and present information about complex medical topics in a structured and accessible manner. These pages are particularly useful when dealing with diseases that encompass a broad spectrum of subtypes, each with distinct characteristics. The purpose of a landing page is to provide a general overview of the disease while linking to more detailed, focused pages that address specific subtypes or aspects of the condition. When to Use Landing Pages Landing pages are most appropriate when a disease entity is extensive or includes multiple subtypes with varying features. In such cases, it can be beneficial to divide the information into smaller, more manageable sections, referred to as microchapters. These microchapters are individual pages that are interconnected through a central landing page. The landing page serves as a hub, offering general information about the disease and directing readers to the specific pages for each subtype. Each of these linked pages delves into the unique details of a particular subtype, such as its epidemiology, risk factors, clinical presentation, diagnostic criteria, and treatment options. These hyperlinks allow readers to easily access related pages and explore the broader context of the disease. While some overlap in content between pages is inevitable, common information can be reused across multiple pages, provided that proper citations are included. Examples of landing pages and their associated microchapters can be found in the provided templates. These examples illustrate different styles of landing pages, including those that link exclusively to microchapter-style pages, those that link to single-page-style content, and those that combine both formats. Examples of Chapters Using Landing Pages Example 1: Colitis Colitis is a broad disease entity characterized by diverse pathophysiological etiologies, such as allergic colitis, infectious colitis, and ulcerative colitis. Each subtype exhibits distinct epidemiological patterns, risk factors, clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and treatment approaches. To effectively present this information, a Colitis landing page was created, serving as a central resource that links to individual chapters for each subtype. In this case, the author identified eight subtypes of colitis. Three of these subtypes are presented in a single-page format, while the remaining five are organized into microchapter-style pages. All pages are interconnected and linked back to the main landing page, ensuring a cohesive and user-friendly structure. Example 2: Pneumonia Pneumonia is another condition that benefits from the use of a landing page. It has two primary subtypes: community-acquired pneumonia and hospital-acquired pneumonia. These subtypes differ significantly in terms of risk factors, underlying causes, and treatment regimens. For instance, the pathogens involved, patterns of microbial resistance, and therapeutic strategies vary between the two. To accurately reflect these differences, a general Pneumonia landing page was created, linking to two microchapter-style pages dedicated to each subtype. This approach allows for a clear and detailed presentation of the unique aspects of each form of pneumonia. Example 3: Endophthalmitis Endophthalmitis is a condition with numerous classifications. Although the differences between these classifications may not be dramatic, the sheer number of subtypes makes it challenging to present all the information on a single page without overwhelming the reader. To address this, a landing page was developed to provide a general overview of endophthalmitis, with links to individual pages for each subtype. This method aligns with the goal of delivering high-quality, easily digestible information to readers, ensuring that complex topics are presented in a clear and accessible manner.
